task.goal: Keep a neighborhood mutual-aid pantry stocked without making donations unpredictable for recipients.
hard_constraints: Three volunteers, one shelf and a weekly inventory count; no cash collection.
Do not display recipient names or reserve food by perceived deservingness.
Track stockouts, spoilage, volunteer time and unmet requests.
task.available_resources: Paper tally and existing donation schedule.
task.expected_result: A workable allocation and replenishment routine.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Recurring staple commitments
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make replenishment more predictable by asking existing donors to commit to specific staple categories on their existing donation dates. Commitments are voluntary gifts of food, never money. This changes the supply mechanism: donors fill recurring gaps instead of independently guessing what to bring.

At the weekly inventory count, one volunteer records usable quantities, spoilage and anonymous unmet requests by category. The three volunteers select a short core list based on observed requests and suitable shelf-stable foods. Set modest weekly targets that fit the single shelf; treat these as planning targets, not guaranteed availability. Ask scheduled donors to choose a category and quantity they can repeat, and to report missed deliveries when possible. Unexpected donations remain welcome if safe and space permits. Publish the actual delivery schedule and clearly distinguish expected donations from food already available.

Use open access with a posted request to take a modest quantity of scarce staples per visit. Apply the same guidance to everyone, without names, eligibility judgments or individual reservations. Put earlier-expiring safe food at the front.

Divide responsibility among donor coordination, shelf care and weekly records, rotating roles if useful. On the paper tally, record each observed stockout and its discovery date, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. An empty category found during the weekly count has an unknown stockout start time; do not imply continuous monitoring.

This requires enough repeat donors willing to make realistic commitments and a way to contact them already associated with the donation schedule. It cannot guarantee supply when commitments fail or demand rises. Start with only a few staples so coordination remains feasible.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use two existing weeks as a comparator, or record two baseline weeks if none exist, then try commitments for four weeks. Compare core-category stockouts and unmet requests alongside delivered quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes. The mechanism is doubtful if commitments repeatedly go unfilled or gaps do not fall despite similar demand and donation volume. Treat a short trial as provisional evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A visible buffer with scheduled releases
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Smooth access across the week by dividing suitable donations between immediate availability and a small, openly explained buffer released on fixed days. The mechanism changes when food becomes available, reducing the chance that a delivery is exhausted immediately and leaves later visitors with nothing.

At the weekly count, estimate the coming week's usable shelf-stable supply. Leave most available immediately and mark a small section of the same shelf as the next scheduled release, using paper labels. Choose release times the three volunteers can reliably cover, preferably during existing donation visits. Publish the times and explain that the buffer belongs to the whole community; nothing is assigned to named recipients. All visitors face the same release rules, and anyone may take food from the available section without a deservingness assessment.

Use the buffer only for durable, commonly requested items. Perishables and food nearing its safe-use limit go directly into circulation. If demand is low or a release would create spoilage, release the buffer early and note the exception. If the shelf cannot clearly distinguish available stock from the buffer, this approach is unsuitable. It also depends on visitors respecting the labels; volunteers should not police identities or maintain recipient lists.

One volunteer leads the weekly count, while the other two handle scheduled releases and shelf care. Record available-section stockouts separately from total depletion: food held for later does not make a present unmet request disappear. Tally spoilage, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests, including requests made while buffer stock remains. Log stockout discovery and refill dates without claiming exact durations.

No storage beyond the one shelf is needed. The main tradeoff is explicit: retaining food for later visitors may deny an immediate request. Keep the buffer small and change or abandon it if that tradeoff worsens access.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare two ordinary weeks with four buffer weeks, alternating approaches if practical. Track unmet requests and stockouts by early versus late week, plus total spoilage and volunteer time. The buffer fails if later access does not improve, total unmet requests increase, or releases are frequently missed. Compare donation quantities and visitor-request tallies before attributing changes to release timing.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Equal flexible shares across food categories
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Stretch scarce staples across more visits through a simple, universal share rule with recipient-chosen substitutions. The mechanism changes allocation: instead of unrestricted early depletion of a popular item, everyone is asked to take the same modest share while choosing among available alternatives.

During the weekly count, group suitable food into a few understandable categories, such as meal bases, proteins and vegetables. Keep foods in their original packaging on the single shelf; no bags or additional storage are required. Post a paper guide such as 'Please start with one item from each available category per visit.' Choose quantities from actual supply, and relax the guidance for abundant items or items nearing expiry. Explain that this is a shared starting allowance, not a nutritionally complete household ration.

Recipients choose their own items and may decline unsuitable food. Clearly labeled alternatives within a category can satisfy different preferences, but never assume they meet an allergy, religious or medical requirement. Record requests for unavailable suitable options as unmet even when other food remains. Do not require names, proof of need or staff judgments about who deserves more. Use a voluntary rule rather than recipient tracking; repeat visits and uneven household needs remain limitations.

Use the existing donation schedule to ask for whichever categories are repeatedly missing. One volunteer prepares the weekly category guidance, another checks safe stock rotation during existing visits, and the third maintains the tally; rotate these duties as desired. Record category and item stockouts, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. Count an empty category as a gap even if the shelf still contains plenty of another category.

This needs understandable categories, enough variety to make choice meaningful and broad cooperation. It may distribute scarce food more widely, but cannot correct insufficient total supply and may be too restrictive for larger households.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare two weeks of the current access routine with four weeks of flexible shares. Examine scarce-item stockouts, anonymous unmet requests, spoilage and volunteer minutes alongside incoming quantities. Add an optional anonymous paper question: 'Could you take food you could use?' Reject or revise the routine if usable access declines, conflicts increase, or scarce items disappear just as quickly under comparable supply.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Spread donation arrivals across the week
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce gaps by moving clustered donation visits to different days on the existing schedule. The mechanism is steadier incoming supply: food reaches the shelf several times during the week, giving later visitors access to fresh arrivals and reducing crowding that can cause spoilage. All delivered food becomes available immediately.

At the weekly inventory count, compare the existing donation schedule with paper records of empty categories and shelf overflow. Ask existing donors whether they can shift their usual delivery to an uncovered part of the week, without increasing their donation or promising particular items. Start by moving just one delivery. Publish agreed delivery windows as expected arrivals, clearly stating that contents and availability can vary. Record cancellations when known; never advertise an expected donation as food already available.

Keep allocation open and consistent: recipients choose from available food, with no names, individual reservations or judgments of deservingness. Place safe, earlier-expiring items at the front. Do not hold back food to make the schedule appear reliable.

One volunteer coordinates schedule changes, one maintains the shelf during already planned visits, and one leads the weekly inventory and tally. Record incoming quantities by broad category, observed stockouts and discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. Leave a paper space for visitors to mark missing items voluntarily. These reports are incomplete observations, not a count of everyone who went without.

This requires clustered arrivals, donors able to change delivery days, and deliveries that do not require extra volunteer trips. It uses the same shelf and paper records. If donations already arrive evenly, donors cannot shift visits, or total supply is inadequate, changing arrival times may offer little benefit.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record two weeks under the current schedule, then try four weeks with one delivery shifted into a recurring gap. Keep ordinary allocation unchanged. Compare late-week observed stockouts and unmet requests, incoming quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes. Also check whether gaps simply move earlier in the week. Reject the change if shifted deliveries are unreliable, require extra trips the volunteers cannot sustain, or show no improvement under roughly comparable supply and reported demand. Sparse reports and changing donation contents limit any conclusion.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Weekly gap slips: replenish what was used or requested
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a weekly feedback rule to direct existing donations toward current gaps. Instead of asking donors for standing staple commitments, give each scheduled donation a short, updated list of missing foods and maximum useful quantities. The mechanism is demand-responsive replenishment: scarce shelf space and donor effort follow actual use and unmet requests, while limits discourage repeated surpluses.

At the weekly count, record usable stock by a few food categories. On the same paper tally, record donations received and anonymous requests for unavailable foods. Estimate consumption from opening stock plus arrivals minus closing stock and recorded spoilage; acknowledge that unrecorded movements make this approximate. For each category, use the previous week's estimated consumption plus unmet requests as an initial weekly target. Subtract usable stock and cap the requested amount at the space available on the single shelf. Volunteers should review unusually large changes rather than automatically amplifying noisy tallies.

Assign each gap to one existing donation slot so multiple donors are not asked to fill the same shortage. Pass the list through the existing scheduling arrangement, or give donors paper slips during their visits for their next delivery. Donors remain free to decline; no purchases, money collection or extra trips are required. Make all safe delivered food immediately available, rotate earlier-expiring food forward, and use open recipient choice without names, reservations or deservingness judgments.

One volunteer counts and calculates gaps, one passes slips through the schedule, and one maintains the tally and shelf during existing visits. Record observed stockouts with discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. Post actual availability separately from requested donations.

This requires donors who can adjust donation contents and reasonably complete arrival records. Weekly feedback can lag sudden demand changes, and cannot overcome insufficient donations. Targets are planning estimates, not promises to recipients.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Record two weeks of ordinary donations, then use gap slips for three weeks. Compare category stockouts and unmet requests alongside incoming quantities, spoilage and volunteer minutes. Inspect whether requested gaps actually receive food and whether surplus categories shrink. Reject or simplify the routine if donors cannot respond before the next count, recordkeeping becomes burdensome, or shortages persist despite comparable total supply and demand. Sparse anonymous tallies limit conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Stagger arrivals while keeping all food available
EXPAND.proposal:
Change the timing of incoming donations so fewer arrive together and more arrive after the shelf usually empties. Unlike recurring staple commitments, this routine coordinates arrival days without asking donors to promise particular foods or quantities. Unlike scheduled releases, every accepted item becomes available immediately.

At the weekly inventory count, mark existing donation days on paper alongside observed stockout discoveries. Ask donors whose visits cluster together whether they can move an existing delivery to an uncovered part of the week. Start by moving only one delivery; do not add trips or assume donors can change their schedules. Publish confirmed donation windows as expected arrivals, clearly distinguished from stock already present. A missed delivery remains a missed delivery, with no availability guarantee.

One volunteer coordinates the paper schedule, one counts and rotates stock, and one maintains records and checks the next delivery during an existing visit. Anyone may take available food without identification, reservations or judgments of deservingness. Keep safe food approaching expiry accessible first. If a donor cancels, mark that arrival unconfirmed and ask whether another already scheduled delivery can move; never conceal a current shortage.

Record quantities received, observed stockouts and discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests by category. Weekly observations cannot establish exact depletion times.

This requires donors with some scheduling flexibility and existing means of contacting them. It can reduce gaps caused by clustered deliveries, but cannot solve inadequate total donations or ensure suitable items arrive. Moving a delivery may also disadvantage people who depend on the original day.
EXPAND.experiment: The schedule volunteer owns a four-week trial moving one existing delivery. Compare with two weeks under the existing schedule or recurring commitments, accounting for incoming quantities. Look for fewer observed gaps and unmet requests across the week. Restore the original day if missed deliveries increase, unmet requests rise, or coordination exceeds 15 extra volunteer minutes weekly. If comparable supply produces no improvement, timing was probably not the main constraint.

EXPAND.title: Prevent slow-moving donations from blocking the shelf
EXPAND.proposal:
Protect scarce shelf capacity by changing which donations enter when space is tight. The mechanism addresses congestion: bulky, rarely taken food can prevent useful replenishment even while recipients report shortages. Recurring staple commitments alone may leave this physical bottleneck unresolved.

At the weekly count, sketch the shelf on paper and identify food that remains from the previous count. Check safety and expiry, keep edible stock available, and note anonymous requests for missing usable foods. Do not equate slow movement with lack of need after a single week. After two counts showing the same blockage, contact the next scheduled donors before they travel: explain the actual space limit and ask them to substitute compact, requested food or postpone that particular bulky donation. Donations remain voluntary and involve no cash.

All accepted food is immediately available to everyone. There are no recipient names, individual reservations or deservingness assessments. Never discard safe food merely to make the shelf appear better stocked. If a donor cannot substitute, accept what safely fits and explain any physical capacity limit; do not assume an alternative storage or redistribution site exists. Stop postponing a category if anonymous requests show that people need it.

One volunteer records shelf occupancy and quantities during the weekly count; another contacts scheduled donors; the third checks rotation and maintains the tally. Track capacity-related refusals or postponements alongside stockouts, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests. Retain ordinary access while testing the change.

This requires recurring congestion, donors reachable before delivery and some flexibility in what they bring. It will not help an already mostly empty shelf. Reducing incoming volume or variety is a real risk, even if the remaining stock turns over faster.
EXPAND.experiment: The inventory volunteer owns a four-week trial affecting only one repeatedly congested shelf section. Compare with ordinary acceptance or recurring staple commitments. Check whether requested food is more often available and unmet requests fall, accounting for total donations and food declined. Stop if the intervention causes a requested category to disappear, spoilage rises, or donor coordination exceeds 15 extra minutes weekly. Faster turnover alone does not count as success.

EXPAND.title: Use an anonymous stockout signal to redirect the next delivery
EXPAND.proposal:
Shorten the delay between an observed shortage and a useful replenishment. Put a small paper signal beside three common staple categories: 'available,' 'empty observed,' or 'replacement requested.' Visitors may mark an empty category or add an anonymous unmet request. Volunteers also record observations during existing visits. A signal reports a problem; it never promises a delivery.

At the weekly count, choose the three categories and reset the paper using actual stock. One volunteer owns follow-up, contacting the next donor on the existing schedule when a shortage is reported. Ask whether that donor can replace part of their planned donation with the missing category. Do not request an extra journey, a standing commitment or money. Mark 'replacement requested' only after making contact, and mark an expected arrival only if the donor confirms. All delivered food goes directly onto the single shelf for unrestricted, anonymous access.

To keep coordination bounded, make at most one donor contact per category between weekly counts. If the donor cannot help or is unreachable, leave the shortage visible and continue ordinary donations. Recipients need provide only a category or a short description of the unavailable suitable food; names, household histories and proof of need are unnecessary. Multiple marks are reports, not verified counts of distinct people.

The other two volunteers cover inventory, safe rotation and recordkeeping. Log stockout discovery and replenishment dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests, including unresolved requests. Weekly counts remain the only scheduled inventory counts.

This requires occasional observations between counts, an existing donor contact channel and donors able to substitute items. Unlike recurring commitments, it responds to actual depletion rather than forecast demand. Its limits are delayed observation, uncertain reports and the possibility that substitutions create a different shortage.
EXPAND.experiment: The follow-up volunteer owns a four-week trial for three categories. Compare with weekly requests through the existing schedule or recurring commitments, recording delivery quantities. Check whether observed shortages are replenished sooner and unmet requests decline. Stop if substitutions repeatedly create other shortages or contacts exceed 15 extra minutes weekly. No improvement after accounting for donor responsiveness and added work favors the simpler weekly routine.

EXPAND.title: Recurring staples with a missed-delivery recovery rule
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade source: “Recurring staple commitments.” Keep voluntary commitments to specific staple categories on existing donation dates, modest shelf-sized targets, anonymous access, safe stock rotation and the distinction between expected food and food actually available. The added action is an everyday response to missed commitments; the source asks donors to report misses but does not specify how to recover.

At the weekly count, three volunteers choose a short core list using usable stock and anonymous unmet requests. One volunteer coordinates donors, one manages shelf condition and one maintains records. Ask existing donors to choose realistic recurring quantities; collect no money. Post actual availability separately from expected arrivals. Apply the same voluntary modest-taking guidance to everyone, without recipient names, reservations or deservingness judgments.

When a missed delivery is reported or discovered during an existing visit, the coordinator marks it unconfirmed and makes at most one recovery contact: ask the next scheduled donor whether they can substitute the missing staple without removing another core item already expected that week. Do not request another trip. The coordinator owns the request until the donor explicitly accepts; silence is not acceptance. If coordination is interrupted, the paper entry remains unresolved and the ordinary donation proceeds. Another volunteer may take over by marking ownership on that entry.

If recovery fails, leave the shortage visible. If the same commitment misses twice consecutively, remove it from next week's expected supply until the donor reconfirms a feasible quantity. Food remains welcome whenever it arrives. This prevents an unreliable promise from repeatedly shaping the plan, although it cannot replace missing supply.

Record quantities received, observed stockouts and discovery dates, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests, including unresolved suitable-food requests. Weekly counts cannot establish exact stockout durations. This requires repeat donors and an existing contact method. Compared with ordinary recurring commitments, recovery may reduce gaps but adds contact work and can displace donations; the substitution boundary limits that risk.
EXPAND.experiment: The donor coordinator runs a four-week trial covering at most three core categories. Use existing records as a comparator if sufficient; otherwise observe two weeks of ordinary commitments first. Record missed commitments, accepted recovery requests and actual replacement deliveries alongside all required measures. Limit recovery work to 15 additional volunteer minutes per week; when the limit is reached, leave remaining gaps visible and follow the ordinary schedule. Stop recovery substitutions if they cause another core shortage twice, or if unmet requests rise across comparable weeks without a clear supply explanation. Retain simple commitments if recovery adds work without useful deliveries. Short observations and changing demand limit causal conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Stagger donations only after protecting the original day's access
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade source: “Stagger arrivals while keeping all food available.” Preserve its mechanism of moving an existing delivery into a gap, immediate access to every accepted item, one-delivery trial, public expected-arrival information and rollback. The added decision rule addresses displacement: moving food can improve later access by creating an earlier shortage, and the source acknowledges this risk without a routine safeguard.

During the weekly inventory count, one volunteer reviews the existing schedule, stockout observations and anonymous requests. Consider moving one delivery only when records show a gap later in the week and another delivery is still scheduled in the original window. If records are insufficient, keep the schedule and collect observations during existing visits for two weeks. Do not add counts or trips.

The schedule volunteer asks whether the donor can move an existing visit. The original date remains in force until the donor explicitly accepts the new date; the volunteer owns the change through acceptance and records it on paper. Publish only accepted changes as expected arrivals, never guaranteed stock. If that volunteer becomes unavailable before acceptance, another volunteer can read the unresolved entry and continue it; otherwise retain the original schedule.

After a move, an observed core-category stockout or unmet request in the vacated window triggers review at the next weekly count. Restore the original date for the next delivery if the remaining original-window donation failed, or if early-window unmet requests increased without an offsetting reduction later. Obtain the donor's acceptance before publishing restoration. If neither date is feasible, mark the delivery unconfirmed and plan from remaining confirmed arrivals.

The other volunteers handle shelf rotation and records. Everyone may take available food anonymously; there are no individual reservations or deservingness judgments. Record incoming quantities, stockouts and discovery dates, spoilage, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests by early or late week. This needs flexible, reachable donors and enough observations to distinguish the two windows. Compared with unrestricted rescheduling, the safeguard may forgo a useful move, but reduces the risk of merely relocating the shortage.
EXPAND.experiment: The schedule volunteer trials one accepted move for four weeks after two recorded weeks on the original schedule, unless adequate records already exist. Compare early- and late-week unmet requests and observed stockouts, accounting for delivered quantities; also compare spoilage and volunteer minutes. Use the operational restoration rule immediately when triggered. End the trial if coordination exceeds 15 extra minutes weekly or delivery reliability worsens. Keep the change only if later access improves without an apparent larger loss earlier. With sparse observations, retain the original schedule rather than claim an improvement.

EXPAND.title: Ask for food recipients can use as received
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: improve the usable share of donations by removing preparation requirements that some recipients cannot meet. A shelf can contain food while remaining effectively unavailable to someone without a cooker, can opener or suitable storage. This route changes food suitability at the existing donation decision, rather than donation timing, recurring quantities, release timing or recipient shares.

At the weekly count, record anonymous unmet requests with an optional practical reason: for example, 'needs food edible without cooking' or 'cannot open this packaging.' Do not ask for identities or personal histories. Count these as unmet even if other food remains. Absence of reports does not establish that everyone can use the stock.

One volunteer coordinates the next scheduled donation. When an explicit usability request exists, ask that donor whether a small part of their planned donation can instead be a suitable shelf-stable, ready-to-eat item in accessible packaging. Specify the practical requirement and let the donor decline. Ask during existing coordination, with no money collection, extra trip or standing commitment. Until the donor accepts, the ordinary donation plan continues. If no contact method already exists, make the request at the next donation encounter for a future delivery.

Start with one requested substitution per week. Keep other useful variety and all safe existing stock available; do not reject cooking ingredients simply because some people cannot use them. If the donor cannot substitute, record the request as unresolved. Never claim that a replacement satisfies an allergy or medical requirement without adequate product information.

A second volunteer rotates stock and checks packaging; the third maintains the paper tally. All food is immediately available under ordinary anonymous access, without recipient reservations or deservingness assessments. Track stockouts, spoiled units, volunteer minutes and anonymous unmet requests, separating physical absence from preparation or packaging barriers. Also record whether requested substitutions actually arrived.

This requires recipients to be willing and able to report a barrier and donors to have suitable options. Compared with simply asking for more staples, it may make existing donations useful to more visitors, but could reduce donated quantity or variety. It cannot guarantee nutritionally complete meals or meet every dietary need.
EXPAND.experiment: The records volunteer owns a four-week trial after two weeks recording usability-related requests under ordinary donations. Test only one explicitly requested substitution each week. At the next weekly review, use anonymous reports and remaining stock to inspect whether that barrier persists; disappearance alone does not prove the intended users benefited. Compare usable-food requests, all stockouts, spoilage and volunteer time, alongside donation quantities. Stop substitutions if they repeatedly remove a requested staple, produce unused accumulating stock, or require more than 15 extra volunteer minutes weekly. If no relevant requests appear, make no substitutions and retain ordinary donations.
